dimensions.assessment: Affects the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Federal Reserve, the Treasury, and large financial institutions or potential acquiring banks.
dimensions.evidence: the Corporation may, at the discretion of the Corporation, select an alternative method... that is not the least costly to the Deposit Insurance Fund

dimensions.assessment: Gives federal regulators significant discretion to select more costly bank resolution methods to prevent further market concentration among major banking organizations.
dimensions.evidence: outweighed by the reasonably expected benefits of limiting further concentration of the United States banking system in global systemically important banking organizations.

dimensions.assessment: Permits potential additional risks and costs to the Deposit Insurance Fund up to a maximum cost established by rule, offset by assessments paid by purchasers over time.
dimensions.evidence: maximum allowable cost against the net worth of the Deposit Insurance Fund that may be utilized

dimensions.assessment: Amends the Federal Deposit Insurance Act to carve out an explicit exception to long-standing least-cost resolution mandates and mandates new agency rulemaking.
dimensions.evidence: Section 13(c)(4) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (12 U.S.C. 1823(c)(4)) is amended

dimensions.assessment: Provides a permanent statutory exception for future bank resolutions and requires ongoing compliance rules and post-resolution congressional reports.

missing_information: The specific numerical maximum cost threshold to the Deposit Insurance Fund, which the FDIC is directed to establish by rule later.
importance_detail.rationale: The bill allows the FDIC to bypass the least-cost resolution requirement when handling failing banks under specific conditions intended to limit the concentration of banking assets among global systemically important banks (G-SIBs). It introduces new rule-making, assessments for purchasers, and congressional reporting.

card.summary: The Main Street Capital Access Act modifies and lessens various banking regulations, adjusts capitalization requirements and asset thresholds for community banks and holding companies, and alters federal bank supervision, merger reviews, and resolution procedures.
